title: AICC Voice Gateway
summary: A Voice Gateway that connects real-time phone audio with multiple AI providers. PBX and SIP integration, per-call Workers, and provider-specific protocol and audio differences are separated so one call flow can select the configured implementation.

keyOutcome.label: Key Outcome
keyOutcome.value: Confined provider changes to Transport, Strategy, and Codec boundaries
keyOutcome.description: The core call flow stays stable while configuration selects the required AI provider.

projectIntro.title: Project background
projectIntro.description: Extending the web-first OptiGen conversation experience into phone calls required a separate layer connecting telephony, real-time audio, AI conversations, and speech providers. Voice Gateway owns call state and audio processing so OptiGen's core conversation logic remains separate from the telephone environment.

service.label: System
service.description: A voice relay system connecting real-time phone audio with OptiGen AI conversation requests and responses

flow.label: User flow
flow.description: Convert phone audio through STT, generate an OptiGen AI response, then return it to the call as TTS audio

role.label: My scope
role.description: Voice Gateway design and implementation, PBX and SIP integration, per-call sessions and Workers, audio processing, and AI provider abstraction

problem.title: Problem and requirements
problem.description: The system had to translate phone audio into AI conversations without breaking the call flow and support different speech providers within one service architecture.

realtimeAudio.title: Real-time audio processing
realtimeAudio.description: Call audio had to be received continuously, processed through STT and AI, and returned through TTS without interrupting the conversation.

sessionConsistency.title: Consistent call and conversation state
sessionConsistency.description: Audio, input events, and AI responses for each call had to remain isolated from every other active call.

vendorDifferences.title: Provider-specific differences
vendorDifferences.description: STT and TTS providers use different configuration, streaming, and audio formats, so the core call flow could not depend on one provider.

providerArchitecture.title: Isolating provider protocol and audio differences with Transport and Factory
providerArchitecture.description: I redesigned a structure that required changes across the call flow for every new Voice AI provider into a common contract, configuration-based selection, and provider-specific implementation boundaries.

coupling.title: Problem
coupling.description: A single Voice Client file owned connection handling, event interpretation, STT and TTS, and audio conversion. Adding a provider therefore required changing existing call logic, and STT or TTS could not be replaced independently.

contract.title: Common Transport contract
contract.description: I defined IVoiceTransport for every Voice Client and moved connection state, exponential backoff with jitter, keep-alive, and common error classification into BaseVoiceTransport.

factory.title: Configuration-based factories
factory.description: VoiceTransportFactory selects the Transport from configuration. Separate STT and TTS factories allow implementations to change without modifying the shared call flow.

strategyCodec.title: Strategy and Codec boundaries
strategyCodec.description: Provider-specific event formats live in event strategies, while audio-format differences live in codecs. A new provider is therefore centered on its Transport, Strategy, and Codec.

verification.title: Verified result
verification.description: After a refactor spanning 120 files, the Transport, Factory, Strategy, and Codec boundaries remain in the default branch. Multiple Transport, STT, and TTS implementations are selected through the same factory contracts.

workerDecomposition.title: Reducing WorkerContext from 1,114 lines to 658 and splitting its responsibilities
workerDecomposition.description: Even with one Worker per call, a single object owning every internal responsibility made change impact and failures difficult to trace. I split session, turn, audio, and conversation-data responsibilities into focused modules.

oversizedContext.title: An oversized call context
oversizedContext.description: WorkerContext handled session initialization, turn management, PII processing, the audio pipeline, conversation records, and metrics together, so small changes required reasoning about a wide shared state.

responsibilityBoundary.title: Role-focused modules
responsibilityBoundary.description: Responsibilities moved into a turn manager, PII terminator, audio pipeline manager, session builder, conversation data manager, and TTFP tracker.

callIsolation.title: Preserving call isolation
callIsolation.description: Each call continues to own its session and audio flow in an independent Worker, while modules inside that Worker own only the state and behavior required for their role.

result.title: A smaller change radius
result.description: Provider connection, audio processing, turn management, and persistence changes can now remain within their boundaries instead of spreading across the entire WorkerContext.

design.title: Design and technical decisions
design.description: I separated the responsibilities of telephony, call sessions, OptiGen AI, and speech providers to limit the effect of change in each area.

gatewayBoundary.title: Telephony separated from AI services
gatewayBoundary.description: Voice Gateway translates phone events and audio into OptiGen conversation requests, keeping telephony details out of the AI service.

sessionModel.title: Call-scoped session model
sessionModel.description: Each call owns an independent session and conversation identifier so voice input, AI responses, and connection state stay attached to the correct call.

providerAdapter.title: STT and TTS adapters
providerAdapter.description: Provider-specific configuration and audio processing sit behind common interfaces, allowing providers to be selected or replaced through platform configuration.

implementation.title: Other Contributions
implementation.description: Beyond the two featured architecture cases, I implemented the real-time path from call connection through voice input and AI response playback.

twilio.title: PBX and SIP integration layer
twilio.description: Call start, progress, and end events from phone connections and live audio streams are mapped into per-call Voice Gateway Workers and sessions.

audioPipeline.title: Real-time voice pipeline
audioPipeline.description: Incoming audio is converted into STT text for OptiGen AI, and generated responses are converted into TTS audio and returned to the call stream.

callControls.title: Call control and recovery
callControls.description: I implemented VAD-based silence and background-noise handling, DTMF input, call sessions, and reconnection flows.

providerIntegration.title: Multiple STT and TTS providers
providerIntegration.description: Adapters encapsulate provider-specific configuration and audio formats so the active provider can be chosen from platform settings.

outcome.title: Outcome and reflection
outcome.description: Making Voice Gateway an independent voice layer preserved OptiGen's conversation capabilities while isolating the real-time requirements of phone calls.

voiceExtension.title: AI conversations extended to phone calls
voiceExtension.description: The web-based OptiGen conversation flow can be reused while callers speak their questions and hear AI responses.

providerFlexibility.title: Flexible speech-provider selection
providerFlexibility.description: Abstracted STT and TTS implementations reduce the portion of the core call flow tied to a specific provider.

stableFlow.title: Explicit call-state management
stableFlow.description: Separate call sessions, input state, and reconnection flow make state changes in the real-time voice pipeline traceable.

architecture.title: Real-time voice flow
architecture.description: A call from the PBX and SIP integration layer enters an isolated Worker. Factory selects the configured Transport, while Strategy and Codec handle provider-specific events and audio differences.
architecture.alt: A phone call flows through the PBX and SIP integration layer, a per-call Worker, Transport Factory, Strategy, and Codec to Voice AI providers
architecture.caption: The Voice Gateway separates shared call-flow responsibilities from provider-specific protocol and audio responsibilities.
